item.title: Computing Weighted Set Covers with Heterogeneous Stochastic Oracles: Deadline-Constrained Token Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.26656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study computation in which a probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) uses AI systems, abstracted as heterogeneous stochastic oracles (HSOs), to solve Weighted Set Cover. A pilot study shows that an LLM can outperform weighted greedy. HSOs differ in capabilities, response distributions, latencies, and token costs. We study how the PTM selects HSOs to obtain, by a deadline and with a required success probability, a full cover satisfying a prescribed weight threshold, and we analyze expected token cost. For queries requesting full covers, assuming independent call successes and uninformative failures, we characterize by linear programming the minimum expected token cost for every feasible success probability. An optimal policy randomizes over at most two preselected sequences of oracle batches. Among policies attaining maximum success probability, the expected cost reduction of two-batch selection relative to querying all oracles in one batch is nonnegative and submodular. We construct an FPTAS for near-optimal cost reduction under heterogeneous response-time bounds. Computing an optimal two-batch selection is NP-hard but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm for positive integral expected token costs. For partial-cover responses, the PTM combines returned sets across batches and turns. Once their union covers the universe, it verifies total weight directly or obtains a guarantee from LP-dual tests on retained partial covers. We give one-turn probability, token-cost, and hardness results and adaptive token-cost bounds under per-batch assumptions. A constructed instance shows that residual-guided querying can reduce expected token cost by a factor linear in the number of possible residual subproblems.
item.dc:creator: Jie Wang

item.title: Bayesian Optimal Stopping: Invincible Prophets and Achievable Philosophers
item.description: arXiv:2611.26829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Bayesian optimal stopping: a hidden world $H$ is drawn from $K$ worlds according to a known prior and determines the joint distribution of $n$ observations. A decision-maker selects one observation irrevocably to maximize its value, learning about the world as observations arrive. We compare algorithms against the Bayes-optimal online policy (the philosopher) and the offline optimum (the prophet). Our results show that the philosopher is achievable in that we find a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of the Bayes-optimal policy that runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(|\mathcal{I}|^{\log^* |\mathcal{I}| + 1/\varepsilon} \cdot (1/\varepsilon)^{1/\varepsilon^2})$, where $|\mathcal{I}|$ is the size of the input. By contrast, the prophet is invincible and no algorithm can obtain a competitive ratio that substantially exceeds the worst-case guarantees. When the observations are conditionally independent and identically distributed given $H$, the secretary's rule is $1/e$-competitive. We show that no algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio better than $1/e + 1/\mathrm{poly}(K)$ and this bound is attainable. Our approximation scheme builds on a primal improvement subroutine connecting the two benchmarks. Given an $\alpha$-competitive algorithm against the prophet, we construct an algorithm with a strictly better approximation factor against the philosopher. We randomize between the baseline algorithm and a threshold algorithm based on dual martingales that exploit the Bayesian structure. Each improvement yields a tighter dual martingale, enabling repeated primal-dual updates. We approximate these martingales in polynomial time using importance-weighted Monte Carlo sampling. Dual martingales also establish our upper bound on the competitive ratio and may be useful for more general Bayesian online optimization problems.
item.dc:creator: Alireza AmaniHamedani, Ali Aouad, Senem I\c{s}{\i}k, Thomas Kesselheim, Amin Saberi

item.title: Revisiting Generalized Median Estimators: Exact Bitwise Computation and Gray Code Acceleration
item.description: arXiv:2611.26848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized median estimators evaluate the median of a symmetric kernel over all $M = \binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$. Exhaustive evaluation was considered impractical even for $n = 29, k = 5$ ($M = 118,755$), prompting stochastic subsampling (Wilde and Grimshaw, 2013). We show that this barrier is computational, not combinatorial: storing all subsets requires $\Theta(kM)$ space, whereas stateful enumeration uses $\mathcal{O}(k)$ auxiliary state and retains only $M$ kernel values. We combine two exhaustive traversals with three-way Quickselect and a deterministic median-of-medians fallback, giving worst-case $\mathcal{O}(M)$ selection. Gosper's successor takes $\mathcal{O}(k)$ kernel work per subset for $n < w$; a Revolving Door Gray code changes one element out and one in, enabling $\mathcal{O}(1)$ kernel updates between recalibrations and $\mathcal{O}(M + kM/P)$ total time. We derive floating-point error bounds for the location ($h_1$) and mean-centered sample variance ($h_2$) kernels and their resulting median. For $n = 29, k = 5$, our ANSI C implementation evaluates all $118,755$ subsets in $0.74$ ms and $0.71$ ms, respectively. A direct C sweep places the crossover with partial lexicographic unranking at approximately $18,000$-$23,000$ subsets ($15\%$-$19\%$ of $M$), below the $32,160$-$45,420$ subsets required by Wilde and Grimshaw's sequential approximation at $\epsilon = 0.01$.
item.dc:creator: Robin Nunkesser

item.title: Testable Testing: Distribution-Robust Property Testing
item.description: arXiv:2611.27033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new model for property testing of Boolean functions, which we call distribution-robust testing. Distribution-robust testing is motivated by the hope of designing testers whose output can be trusted even when the underlying probability distribution does not satisfy the assumptions of the tester, while still being more efficient than distribution-free testers that make no assumptions at all. The purpose of this paper is to perform a broad initial exploration of this new model. In particular, we present a variety of general algorithmic techniques, which we apply to show that several well-studied properties admit distribution-robust testers that are significantly more efficient than their distribution-free counterparts. For example, we obtain constant-query distribution-robust testers for conjunctions, decision lists, and unions of intervals, all of which are known to require significantly more queries in the distribution-free model. These encouraging results suggest a range of questions for future work.
item.dc:creator: Xi Chen, Renato Ferreira Pinto Jr., Nathaniel Harms, Rocco A. Servedio

item.title: Distribution-Robust Halfspace Testing
item.description: arXiv:2611.27062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard property testing algorithms are typically designed either for a specific input distribution (distribution-specific algorithms) or for an arbitrary unknown distribution (distribution-free algorithms). Halfspaces are an important example where distribution-specific testers can be extremely efficient, while distribution-free testers are expensive and essentially require learning. We introduce an intermediate type of algorithm, a distribution-robust halfspace tester, which must provide the same guarantees as a distribution-specific tester when the input distribution is the one specified, but must also provide a trustworthy answer under arbitrary distributions. This is achieved by allowing the tester to report that its input distribution is not what it expected (inspired by the recent testable learning framework of Rubinfeld and Vasilyan). We prove that distribution-robust testing of halfspaces under the standard Gaussian requires only $O(n^{2/3})$ queries, compared to the known $\widetilde \Omega(n)$ required for distribution-free testing. We also prove that sample-based distribution-robust testing of halfspaces is harder than sample-based testing under the standard Gaussian, requiring at least $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ samples compared to the known $\widetilde \Theta(\sqrt n)$ bound for the latter. In fact, we show that the latter $\widetilde \Theta(\sqrt n)$ bound becomes $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ when the covariance matrix is only mildly perturbed.
item.dc:creator: Xi Chen, Renato Ferreira Pinto Jr., Nathaniel Harms, Rocco A. Servedio

item.title: Balanced Divide and Conquer for Rooted Maximum Agreement Forests
item.description: arXiv:2611.27160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a balanced divide-and-conquer framework for the maximum agreement forest problem on rooted binary phylogenetic tree--forest instances. The goal is a common subforest with the fewest components; budget $k$ bounds the increase relative to the input forest. We balance edges associated with an unknown optimum to obtain three subproblems with smaller budgets. Branching separates the inputs, while temporary marker leaves allow a global optimum to be recovered from independently computed optimal solutions. For any fixed $B>\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$, the framework converts a tree--forest solver running in $O^*(B^k)$ time into one running in $O^*((\sqrt{\varphi B})^k)$ time. Starting from an $O^*(2.3391^k)$-time solver, two applications yield an $O^*(1.7743^{k^*})$-time fixed-parameter algorithm for two trees, where $k^*$ is the number of components in a maximum agreement forest minus one. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a fixed number of applications yields $O^*((\varphi+\varepsilon)^{k^*})$ time. Here $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors, whose degree and constants may depend on $\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: Feng Shi, Yexin Peng, Xin Zeng, Jingyi Liu, Qilong Feng, Jianxin Wang

item.title: Tight Logarithmic Separations between LZ77 and LZRR
item.description: arXiv:2611.27213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LZRR is a copy-based lossless compression method that produces a bidirectional macro scheme. It greedily parses a string from left to right. At each step, it can copy from an occurrence on either side of the current position, provided that the copy creates no cycle. Let $z$ and $z_{\mathrm{RR}}$ denote the sizes of the LZ77 and LZRR parsings, respectively. Under the original LZRR rule, we show that $z/z_{\mathrm{RR}}=\Theta(\log n)$ on a family of Fibonacci words and that $z_{\mathrm{RR}}/z=\Theta(\log n)$ on a family based on bit reversal, where $n$ is the string length. The Fibonacci separation holds under every tie-breaking rule. Both separations are asymptotically tight.
item.dc:creator: Yuto Fujie

item.title: Space-Efficient Text Indexing for Advanced Counting Queries
item.description: arXiv:2611.27432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the classical problem of text indexing, the objective is to preprocess a text $T=T[1..n]$ over an integer alphabet $[0..\sigma)$ into a data structure that supports efficient pattern matching queries. Given a pattern $P=P[1..m]$, a reporting query lists the set $\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)$ of occurrences of $P$ in $T$, whereas a counting query returns $|\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)|$. Space-efficient suffix-tree variants use only $\mathcal{O}(n\log\sigma)$ bits and support reporting queries in $\mathcal{O}(m+|\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)|\cdot\log_{\sigma}^{\epsilon} n)$ time, where $\epsilon>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant, and counting queries in $\mathcal{O}(m)$ time. Notably, space-efficient indexes for more advanced counting queries have largely resisted achieving the same optimal (or near-optimal) query times when using less than $\Theta(n\log n)$ bits. We change this situation by proposing a general framework that supports advanced counting queries, denoted by $\phi_T(P)$, provided that $\phi_T$ satisfies two mild conditions: (1) $\phi_T(P)$ is an integer in $[0..|\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)|]$ that can be computed from $\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)$ via sorting; and (2) $\phi_T(Q)\geq\phi_T(P)$ for every prefix $Q$ of $P$. We show that our framework supports optimal $\mathcal{O}(m)$-time queries using $\mathcal{O}(n\log\sigma+n(\log\log n)^2)$ bits or near-optimal $\mathcal{O}(m\log_{\sigma}^{\epsilon} n)$-time queries using $\mathcal{O}(n\log\sigma)$ bits. As an example, our trade-offs improve upon the classical MAST index for counting non-overlapping occurrences [Apostolico and Preparata, Algorithmica, 1996; Brodal et al., ICALP 2002], which uses $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ bits and supports $\mathcal{O}(m)$-time queries, and the recent compact index for the same problem [Bals et al., ESA 2026], which uses $\mathcal{O}(n\log\sigma)$ bits and supports $\mathcal{O}(m\log n\log_{\sigma}^{\epsilon} n)$-time queries.
item.dc:creator: Solon P. Pissis, Sharma V. Thankachan

item.title: Shellsort with $O(n\log n)$ Average-Case Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.27671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that Shellsort admits a fixed sequence of $O(\log n)$ gaps that sorts a uniform random permutation in $O(n\log n)$ expected comparisons. In fact, we give a distribution on decreasing gap sequences with this expected bound for every fixed input. We also give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, with high probability, constructs a sequence attaining the average-case bound.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Du, Zongqi Wan

item.title: Kidney Exchange in Deterministic $O^*(4^{t+o(t)})$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.27841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kidney exchange admits a randomized $O^*(4^t)$ algorithm parameterized by the target number $t$ of transplants, but the best previous deterministic algorithm requires $O^*(6.855^t)$ time. We nearly close this gap by developing a deterministic $O^*(4^{t+o(t)})$ algorithm. Our approach uses Dynamic Representative Sets to execute the semi-feasible packing recurrence under a global cardinality budget of $2t$, exploiting a residual extension-budget invariant to avoid repeated static representative-family compression. To handle admissible cycles containing at least $t$ vertices, we establish a deterministic $O^*(4^{k+o(k)})$ algorithm for finding a shortest simple directed cycle of length at least $k$. Beyond feasibility, our framework supports additive optimization, yielding the same running-time bound for maximizing arc utility among packings with exactly $t$ transplants. Consequently, a packing that lexicographically maximizes the number of transplants and then additive utility can be computed deterministically in $O^*(4^{\tau+o(\tau)})$ time, where $\tau$ is the maximum achievable number of transplants.
item.dc:creator: Binh T. Nguyen

item.title: Geometrically Constrained Learning I: Agnostically Learning Adversarially Robust Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.27852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study agnostic learning under the Gaussian distribution with guarantees on both classification error and robustness to adversarial perturbations. We say that a function has boundary profile $K \ge 1$ if, for all $r > 0$, the probability that a point lies within Euclidean distance $r$ of the classification boundary is at most $Kr$. We give an algorithm that takes a robustness radius parameter $r$ and learns a hypothesis with boundary volume $O(Kr)$ and classification error $\mathsf{opt}_K + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}_K$ is the minimum classification error among functions with boundary profile at most $K$. For general $r$, $K$, and $\varepsilon$, the algorithm runs in time $d^{\widetilde{O}(K^2/\varepsilon^2 + K^4r^2/\varepsilon^4)}$. In particular, in the $Kr = O(\varepsilon)$ regime, the algorithm runs in time $d^{\widetilde{O}(K^2/\varepsilon^2)}$. Up to logarithmic factors in the exponent, this matches the statistical query lower bound for agnostically learning the $K$-profile class without recovering robustness. For natural geometric classes, including convex sets and Boolean combinations of halfspaces, this matches the corresponding surface-area-based running-time bound for non-robust agnostic learning via $L_1$ polynomial regression, up to logarithmic factors in the exponent. Our algorithm performs $L_1$ error minimization over polynomials, with an auxiliary coordinate roughly standing in for distance to the boundary. A convex constraint on the gradient of the polynomial, in this $(d+1)$-dimensional space, produces local certificates of the range of the polynomial on balls of radius $r$. Our algorithm finds a polynomial such that these certified ranges are small, then obtains a robust classifier via randomized rounding and partitioning of the domain.
item.dc:creator: Jane Lange, Cassandra Marcussen, Arsen Vasilyan

item.title: Linear-Size Spectral Sparsification by Sign Descent
item.description: arXiv:2611.27907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given an undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and arbitrary positive weights, we construct a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-spectral sparsifier with $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ edges. For every $0<\varepsilon<1$, the algorithm succeeds with high probability and runs in time \[ O\!\left(n+\varepsilon^{-3}\bigl[m\log^2 n+n\log^3 n\,(\log\log n)^4\bigr]\right). \] In each phase we seek a reweighting that brings many edge weights to zero or twice their current value while keeping the relative change in every graph energy small. Reversing the weight changes preserves the error and exchanges deletion with doubling, so one choice deletes at least half the edges that reach an endpoint. We balance a smooth penalty for spectral error against a linear reward for alignment with independent random signs. Each step changes the free weights by a fixed fraction of their values at the start of the phase, with directions chosen from the estimated signs of the negative gradient. A weight stays fixed once it reaches an endpoint. We show that while few weights are fixed, the remaining edges admit a direction whose gain in reward exceeds its first-order spectral cost by a constant. The objective is bounded below, so this decrease forces a constant fraction of the weights to an endpoint. We repeat the partial coloring on the surviving edges, choosing the tolerances to keep the total relative error within $\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: Trevor Vaughn

item.title: The Benefit of Migration in Throughput Maximization on Unrelated Machines and under Restricted Assignment
item.description: arXiv:2611.27918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In preemptive throughput maximization on parallel machines, jobs have release dates, due dates and weights, and the goal is to maximize the total weight of the jobs completed by their due dates. We study the benefit of migration, i.e., by what factor the optimal weight can increase when a preempted job is allowed to resume on a different machine. By a classic result of Kalyanasundaram and Pruhs, on identical machines the migratory optimum is at most $O(1)$ times the nonmigratory optimum. We give, for the first time, bounds for unrelated machines and for restricted assignment. We show that on unrelated machines, when every eligible machine can complete a job by itself, the migratory optimum is at most $O(\sqrt n)$ times the nonmigratory optimum, where $n$ is the number of jobs. Under restricted assignment it is at most $O(\log n)$ times the nonmigratory optimum. We provide instances which show that both bounds are best possible up to constant factors, even when the jobs have unit weights. Since our proofs are constructive, we obtain the first nontrivial approximation algorithms for migratory throughput maximization on unrelated machines and under restricted assignment.
item.dc:creator: George Karakostas, Stavros G. Kolliopoulos

item.title: The Power of Sampling for Finding Far-Apart Bases in Matroids
item.description: arXiv:2611.27934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the geometry of matroids via the \emph{diameter} and \emph{dispersion} of the metric space of their bases. Given a matroid $M$, we ask if the diameter of its basis-exchange graph $\mathcal{G}(M)$ can be approximated by sampling two uniformly random bases. As our main result, we show that their expected distance is always at least $1/16$ of the diameter of $\mathcal{G}(M)$. While this might appear to follow from the edge-expansion properties established by Anari, Liu, Gharan and Vinzant (STOC'19), we show that this inutition is false by constructing a graph $G$ with edge-expansion at least $1$ for which sampling two random vertices does \emph{not} give a constant-factor approximation to its diameter. We turn to finding $k\geq 2$ maximally-diverse bases of a matroid, the $k$ (max--min) diversity problem. When $k=2$, the problem is solvable via matroid intersection. However, for $k\geq 3$ no polynomial-time approximation or hardness is known, even for diverse spanning trees. We show that sampling $k\geq 3$ bases provides a tight $\Theta(\log k)$ approximation. We then combine structural insights about the local density of $\mathcal{G}(M)$ with classical LP-rounding techniques to obtain a polynomial-time $1/6$-approximation algorithm for the $k$-diversity problem in arbitrary matroids, the first constant-factor polynomial-time approximation for max--min diversity on any matroid. A key ingredient for our result is the \emph{Farthest Matroid Basis} problem: given a collection of bases, find a new basis as far as possible from all of them. We give a polynomial-time $1/3$-approximation algorithm for this, which is our main algorithmic primitive for $k$ max--min diversity. We also show it is $W[1]$-hard when parameterized by the optimal distance. We also improve the $1/6$-approximation for $k$-diversity, for partition matroids and graphic matroids of constant arboricity.
item.dc:creator: Mayank Goswami, Vasilis Livanos, Pasin Manurangsi, Arturo Merino, GiBeom Park, Adarsh Srinivasan

item.title: One partition function call to rule them all: Efficiently computing the equilibrium landscape of multiple nucleic acid strands
item.description: arXiv:2611.27945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the nearest neighbour model of DNA/RNA binding, the partition function (PF) is a sum of Boltzmann-weighted free energies of the exponentially large set of secondary structures. Dirks et al. [SIAM review, 2007] gave a polynomial time PF algorithm for $O(1)$ strands, generalising McCaskill [Biopolymers, 1990] single-stranded case. Despite the intuition that PF may somehow encode the entire state space, thus far different approaches were required to solve various energy-landscape prediction problems. For example: finding the minimum free energy (MFE), structure(s) for $O(1)$ strands was open since 2007, and we recently solved [ICALP, 2025] via new techniques. We asked if there is a magnifiable PF algorithm [DNA31, 2025], which we answer here in the affirmative. We give an $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space algorithm, for $c=O(1)$ strands of $N$ bases, the same overhead as Dirks et al. (non-magnifiable) algorithm. However, we show that magnification allows for efficient decoding of the entire landscape, concretely: a single call to the magnifiable PF efficiently solves and improves upon a large number of problems, giving: - MFE in $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space; a considerable improvement over our $O(N^4(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^4)$ space result [ICALP 2025]. - The first polynomial time algorithm for the multi-stranded density of states problem, in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space. - The first polynomial time algorithm outputting the entire list of energy levels occupied by at least one structure (in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space), and the first algorithms for various energy landscape and counting problems. Our approach unifies the field of energy landscape prediction showing that a single, general, algorithmic framework neatly unifies a large collection of problems that practitioners care about, and required distinct techniques with worse time bounds.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Shalaby, Damien Woods

item.title: Cluster Editing in Subexponential Fixed-Parameter Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.27956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cluster Editing asks whether at most $k$ edge additions and deletions turn a given $n$-vertex graph into a disjoint union of cliques. For more than a decade, the fastest algorithm for it was the golden-ratio algorithm of B\"ocker with running time $O(1.62^k+n^{O(1)})$. Cao and Chen had conjectured that the subexponential running time $2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$ is possible, but this contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). Recently, the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT of OpenAI and Anthropic refuted ETH itself. Our main result transfers running times from 3-SAT to Cluster Editing. If 3-SAT on formulas with $m$ clauses can be decided in time $T(m)$, then there is an algorithm that, given a graph with $n$ vertices and integers $k$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le k^{1/3}$, decides Cluster Editing in time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot T(2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$. Combined with the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT, this proves Cao and Chen's conjecture, as it solves Cluster Editing in time $2^{O(k\cdot(\log\log\log k)^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log k})}\cdot n^{O(1)}=2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$. The key ingredient is a sparsification theorem for Cluster Editing, the counterpart of the Sparsification Lemma for satisfiability: In time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$, it reduces a given instance to $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}$ weighted instances with $O(rk)$ vertices and degree $O(r)$, each of which is equivalent to a 3-SAT formula with $2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k$ clauses. Conversely, by a known reduction with linear blow-up, every saving in the exponent for Cluster Editing is, up to constant factors, a saving for 3-SAT.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Firbas, Manuel Sorge

item.title: Testability of Homomorphism Inadmissibility: Property Testing Meets Database Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.26861v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we utilize the perspective of property testing to consider the testability of relational database queries. A primary motivation is the desire to avoid reading an entire database to decide a property thereof. We focus on conjunctive queries, which are the most basic and heavily studied database queries. Each conjunctive query can be represented as a relational structure $\mathbf{A}$ such that deciding if the conjunctive query is satisfied by a relational structure $\mathbf{B}$ is equivalent to deciding if there exists a homomorphism from $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$. We phrase our results in terms of homomorphisms. Precisely, we study, for each relational structure $\mathbf{A}$, the testability of homomorphism inadmissibility from $\mathbf{A}$. We consider algorithms that have oracle access to an input relational structure $\mathbf{B}$ and that distinguish, with high probability, the case where there is no homomorphism from $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$, from the case where one needs to remove a constant fraction of tuples from $\mathbf{B}$ in order to suppress all such homomorphisms. We provide a complete characterization of the structures $\mathbf{A}$ from which one can test homomorphism inadmissibility with one-sided error by making a constant number of queries to $\mathbf{B}$. Our characterization shows that homomorphism inadmissibility from $\mathbf{A}$ is constant-query testable with one-sided error if and only if the core of $\mathbf{A}$ is $\alpha$-acyclic. We also show that the injective version of the problem is constant-query testable with one-sided error if $\mathbf{A}$ is $\alpha$-acyclic; this result generalizes existing results for testing subgraph-freeness in the general graph model.
item.dc:creator: Hubie Chen, Yuichi Yoshida

item.title: Online Learning for Minimizing Maximum Tardiness in Single-Machine Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2611.27067v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study online learning for minimizing maximum tardiness (\OMMT) in single-machine scheduling. In each round, the learner selects a permutation of \(n\) fixed jobs, representing a schedule. The environment then reveals a processing time and a due date for each job, and the learner incurs a vector-valued loss whose components correspond to the tardiness of the individual jobs. The goal of the learner is to minimize \(\alpha\)-regret, the difference between the learner's maximum cumulative tardiness and \(\alpha\) times that of the best fixed permutation in hindsight, for as small \(\alpha\) as possible. We investigate OMMT under both stochastic and adversarial environments. In the stochastic setting, we prove that the expected \(1\)-regret of the Follow-the-Leader (FTL) algorithm is \( O\!\left(\frac{n\log n}{\Delta^2}\right) \), together with a corresponding high-probability bound, where \(\Delta\) is a distribution-dependent gap parameter. At round \(t \in \{1,\dots,T\}\), FTL runs in \(O(tn^2)\) time and \(O(tn)\) space. In the adversarial setting, we prove that, for any \(0<c<\log_2 n/16\), the \(\alpha\)-regret is \(\Omega(T)\) whenever \(\alpha<\log_2 n/16-c\). We then reduce OMMT to a surrogate online learning problem and apply Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL), obtaining an expected \(\alpha\)-regret bound of \(O(n^2\sqrt{T})\) for \(\alpha=O(\log n)\). Thus, the logarithmic dependence of \(\alpha\) on \(n\) is tight up to constant factors. Each FTPL update admits a mixed-integer programming formulation whose size is polynomial in \(n\) and \(t\).
item.dc:creator: Yiyang Chen, Kohei Hatano, Eiji Takimoto

item.title: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Regret in Online Convex Optimization and Applications to Contextual Search and Online Inverse Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27572v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give small-loss regret bounds for online convex optimization (OCO), using one subgradient per round. Let $\Delta_T^\star$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed decision in hindsight, measured relative to the per-round minima. Our algorithm achieves the regret bound $O(1+\sqrt{\Delta_T^\star})$ without knowing $\Delta_T^\star$, up to domain and gradient-scale factors. The bound is minimax optimal, including its domain dependence, on $\ell_p$ balls for every $1\le p\le\infty$. No smoothness or condition bounding gradient norms by loss values is assumed, and neither loss values nor the time horizon are needed. Algorithmically, we extend the metric-update revocation of Gupta et al. (2026), originally developed for online inverse optimization, to general OCO using the follow-the-regularized-leader framework and a mixture of multiple base learners. We also apply our algorithm to contextual search and online inverse optimization. In $d$-dimensional contextual search with comparison flips of unknown bias $\kappa>0$, we obtain minimax expected cumulative absolute error $\Theta(\sqrt{d}/\kappa^2)$ under Euclidean normalization using polynomially many arithmetic operations, resolving an open question of Liu et al. (2021). For online inverse optimization with the Euclidean unit-ball utility domain, our algorithm bounds the regret relative to observed actions by $O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\sqrt{D_T})$, where $D_T$ is their cumulative suboptimality; this matches the regret rate of Gupta et al. (2026) when $D_T=0$. Our guarantee extends to other utility domains; for example, on the probability simplex, the bound improves to $O(\log(d+1)+\sqrt{D_T\log(d+1)})$.
item.dc:creator: Shinsaku Sakaue

item.title: Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.27700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz function, $\lambda \ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $\lambda$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. The sample complexity, running time, and representation size are \[ (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(\lambda/\varepsilon)}. \] The learning algorithm can be made \emph{agnostic}, given a known bound on the variance of the label marginal distribution. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. For arbitrary labels with variance at most $V^2 \ge 1$, the complexity is \[ (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(V\lambda/\varepsilon)}, \] and the error is $\mathsf{opt} + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}$ is the minimal error among Lipschitz approximators. Our approach combines $L_1$ polynomial regression under a convex gradient constraint with local correction of the Lipschitz property. The learner finds a polynomial that, after smoothing and clipping its range, is very close to a canonical Lipschitz correction of itself, the lower Lipschitz envelope. Our local corrector modifies the lower envelope by replacing distances to sublevel sets with a Gaussian sampling proxy, allowing the construction to be locally and stably estimated from samples.
item.dc:creator: Jane Lange, Cassandra Marcussen, Arsen Vasilyan

item.title: Hypercube LSH for approximate near neighbors
item.description: arXiv:1702.05760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A celebrated technique for finding near neighbors for the angular distance involves using a set of random hyperplanes to partition the space into hash regions [Charikar, STOC 2002]. Experiments later showed that using a set of orthogonal hyperplanes, thereby partitioning the space into the Voronoi regions induced by a hypercube, leads to even better results [Terasawa and Tanaka, WADS 2007]. However, no theoretical explanation for this improvement was ever given, and it remained unclear how the resulting hypercube hash method scales in high dimensions. In this work, we provide explicit asymptotics for the collision probabilities when using hypercubes to partition the space. Vectors at angle $\pi/3$ collide with probability $(\sqrt{3}/\pi)^{d + o(d)}$ in dimension $d$, compared to $(2/3)^d$ for random hyperplanes, and near-parallel vectors collide with similar asymptotic probabilities in both cases. The limiting exponential base tends continuously to zero as the angle approaches $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from below. For fixed near and far angular thresholds below $\pi/2$, these asymptotics determine the limiting LSH collision-probability ratio $\rho$. We further describe how to use hypercube LSH in practice. A direct partial-hypercube analysis gives a heuristic lattice-sieving time bound $2^{0.3347d+o(d)}$.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 42nd International Symposium on Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science (MFCS 2017), pp. 7:1-7:20, 2017
item.dc:creator: Thijs Laarhoven

item.title: Revisiting the Graph Isomorphism Problem with Semidefinite Programming
item.description: arXiv:1908.06320v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is well-known that two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on $n$ vertices are isomorphic if and only if their compatibility graph, an auxiliary graph on $n^2$ vertices, contains a clique of order $n$. In this paper, we give an exact conic formulation of this clique problem. We show that $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic if and only if a system of linear constraints over the cone of completely positive matrices is feasible. Since deciding membership in the completely positive cone is NP-hard, this formulation does not by itself yield an efficient algorithm. Relaxing complete positivity to positive semidefiniteness yields a semidefinite program whose infeasibility certifies that the two graphs are not isomorphic. We establish basic properties of this relaxation. Specifically, it is at least as strong as the necessary condition given by the Lov\'asz $\vartheta$ number of the complement of the compatibility graph, it never admits a strictly feasible solution, and it is implied by the degree-two level of the Lasserre hierarchy applied to a natural integer formulation of graph isomorphism. In light of known lower bounds for the Lasserre hierarchy, the latter indicates that the relaxation cannot decide isomorphism for all pairs of graphs. We leave open the question of characterizing the pairs of graphs for which the relaxation is tight.
item.dc:creator: Giannis Nikolentzos, Michalis Vazirgiannis

item.title: Space-Efficient Interior Point Method, with applications to Linear Programming and Maximum Weight Bipartite Matching
item.description: arXiv:2009.06106v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of solving linear programs in the streaming model. Given a constraint matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and vectors $b\in\mathbb{R}^m, c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we develop a space-efficient interior point method that optimizes solely on the dual program. To this end, we obtain efficient algorithms for various different problems. For general linear programs whose feasible region lies in a ball of radius $R$ and contains a ball of radius $r$ with known center, we can solve them in $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\log(mR^2\|c\|_2/(r\epsilon)))$ passes and $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ space for an $\epsilon$-approximate solution. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most efficient LP solver in streaming with no polynomial dependence on $m$ for both space and passes. For bipartite graphs, we can solve the minimum vertex cover and maximum weight matching problems (with polynomially bounded integer weights) in $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{m})$ passes and $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space. In addition to our space-efficient IPM, we also give algorithms for solving SDD systems and the isolation lemma in $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space, which are the cornerstones for our graph results.
item.dc:creator: S. Cliff Liu, Zhao Song, Hengjie Zhang, Lichen Zhang, Tianyi Zhou

item.title: Faster algorithms for packing forests in graphs and related problems
item.description: arXiv:2409.20314v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider several problems related to packing forests in graphs. The first one is to find $k$ edge-disjoint forests of maximum size in a directed graph $G$ such that the indegree of each vertex in these forests is at most $k$. We describe a min-max characterization for this problem and show that it can be solved in almost linear time for fixed $k$, extending the algorithm of [Gabow, 1995]. Specifically, the complexity is $O(k \delta m \log n)$, where $n, m$ are the numbers of vertices and edges in $G$, respectively, and $\delta = \max\{1, k - k_G\}$, where $k_G$ is the edge connectivity of the graph. Using our solution to this problem, we obtain algorithms for two applications: (1) The $k$-forest problem: find $k$ forests in an undirected graph $G$ maximizing the number of edges in their union. We show how to solve this problem in $O(k^3 \min\{kn, m\} \log^2 n + k \cdot{\rm MAXFLOW}(m, m) \log n)$ time, breaking the $O_k(n^{3/2})$ complexity barrier of previously known approaches. (2) The Directed edge-connectivity augmentation problem: find a smallest set of directed edges whose addition to the given directed graph makes it strongly $k$-connected. We give a deterministic algorithm with complexity $O(k \delta m \log n)+T_{\rm split}$, where $T_{\rm split}$ is the time to split off one vertex in a graph with $O(m+\delta n)$ edges while preserving strong connectivity among the original vertices. For Eulerian directed graphs, the total complexity is $O(k \delta m \log n)$. A similar approach solves the undirected version of the problem in $O(k \delta m \log n)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Pavel Arkhipov, Vladimir Kolmogorov

item.title: LZD-style Compression Scheme with Truncation and Repetitions
item.description: arXiv:2505.00970v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lempel-Ziv-Double (LZD) is a variation of the LZ78 compression scheme that achieves better compression on repetitive datasets. Nevertheless, prior research has identified computational inefficiencies and a weakness in its compressibility for certain datasets. In this paper, we introduce LZD+, an enhancement of LZD, which enables expected linear-time online compression by allowing truncated references. To address the compressibility weakness exhibited by a lower bound example, we propose LZDR}(LZD-runlength compressed), a further enhancement on top of LZD+, which introduces a repetition-based factorization rule while maintaining linear expected time complexity for offline compression. Both time bounds can be de-randomized by a lookup data structure like a balanced search tree with a logarithmic dependency on the alphabet size. We prove that LZD+ and LZDR, like LZD, have an approximation ratio of $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ with respect to the smallest grammar, already on a single family of binary strings. Conversely, all three produce $O(n^{2/3}\delta^{1/3})$ factors, where $\delta$ is the substring complexity of the text. Additionally, we present three flexible parsing variants of LZDR that yield fewer factors in practice; for one of them, we prove that it never yields more factors than greedy LZDR. Comprehensive benchmarking on standard corpora reveals that LZD+, LZDR, and its flexible variants outperform existing LZ-based methods in the number of factors while keeping competitive runtime efficiency. However, we note that the difference in the number of factors becomes marginal for large datasets like those of the Pizza&Chili corpus.
item.dc:creator: Linus G\"otz, Dominik K\"oppl

item.title: Faster PBWT prefix-array access via batching
item.description: arXiv:2605.15819v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The positional Burrows-Wheeler Transform (PBWT) is commonly used to store haplotype panels compactly in such a way that, given a query haplotype, we can quickly find the set-maximal exact matches (SMEMs) between the query and the haplotypes in a panel. There are generally two steps in this process: first we find the maximal substrings of the query that occur in the same positions in haplotypes in the panel and then, for each such substring, report the IDs of the haplotypes in the panel in which the substring occurs in the same position as in the query. Very recently, Bonizzoni, Gagie and Gao (2026) gave two time-space tradeoffs for the second step: they use either $O ((r + h) \log n)$ bits and $O (\log \log_w \min (h, \ell) + k)$ time to report $k$ haplotype IDs, or $O (r \log h + h \log n)$ bits and $O (k \log \log_w h)$ time, where $r$ is the number of runs in the panel's PBWT, $h$, $\ell$ and $n = h \ell$ are the panel's height, length and size, respectively, and $w$ is the number of bits in a machine word. We observe here that if we can batch queries until we have found $r \lg (h) / \lg r$ such substrings, then for the second step we can easily use $O (r \log h)$ bits and $O (r + K)$ total time to report all $K$ haplotype IDs, which is $O (\log (r) / \log h)$ amortized time for each haplotype ID, assuming the haplotypes in the panel are distinct. With that assumption, this is the same space bound as for Bonizzoni, Gagie and Gao's second tradeoff, with a time bound that is asymptotically smaller when $\lg (r) / \lg h \in o (\log \log_w h)$. Compared to their first tradeoff, our space bound is smaller by a factor of about $\lg (n) / \lg h$ and our time bound is larger by a factor of at most $\lg (r) / \lg h$. Our approach is based on an algorithm for constructing the prefix arrays quickly from the PBWT, which may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie

item.title: Matroid Contention Resolution with Concentration
item.description: arXiv:2607.09268v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Contention resolution schemes (CRS) are widely used for rounding fractional solutions subject to combinatorial constraints. Their guarantees are typically in expectation. Such guarantees alone do not ensure that covering constraints hold, limiting the applicability to problems with covering requirements. We prove lower-tail concentration bounds for the random-order CRS of Adamczyk and W{\l}odarczyk (AW) under the intersection of $k$ matroid constraints. For every linear function with coefficients in $[0,1]$,the output attains nearly the fractional value divided by $k+1$ with failure probability exponentially small in this benchmark,independently of the ground-set size. We extend this bound to normalized monotone submodular functions: the fractional value is given by the multilinear extension, and the concentration bound accounts for the largest singleton value. These guarantees apply to both objectives and covering requirements. Our analysis bounds the fractional value lost in each update and applies a general gain--loss concentration theorem whose bounds are independent of the number of updates. We apply these bounds to obtain new approximation guarantees for matroid intersection coloring and for monotone submodular maximization under matroid, packing, and covering constraints.
item.dc:creator: Marek Adamczyk, Stephen Arndt, Benjamin Moseley, Kirk Pruhs, Michael Zlatin

item.title: A General Framework for Metropolis-Adjusted Dikin Walks: Dimension-Square Mixing on Polytopes and Log-Det Walks on Spectrahedra
item.description: arXiv:2608.25273v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sampling from a log-concave density over a convex body is a fundamental problem. The Metropolis-adjusted Dikin walk draws Gaussian proposals shaped by a local barrier metric, and the main difficulty in its analysis is to control the proposal determinant and the reverse quadratic form at a random endpoint. In this paper, we analyze these walks with exact metrics by keeping the two terms together. In the complete logarithmic acceptance ratio, their leading uncentered terms cancel, and second-order tools control the remaining centered fluctuations. For a polytope given by $n$ inequalities and a convex $L$-Lipschitz potential, we show that the regularized Lee--Sidford walk mixes from a warm start in $\widetilde O((d^{2}+dL^{2}R^{2})\log(w/\delta))$ steps. For a spectrahedron with $n\times n$ blocks, we show that the log-det walk scaled by $\kappa=\widetilde O(\psi^\star)$ mixes in $\widetilde O((\psi^\star nd+dL^{2}R^{2})\log(w/\delta))$ steps, where $\psi^\star$ measures matrix leverage. Both analyses share an acceptance-to-mixing reduction. Moreover, we give exact-arithmetic implementations. For polytopes, a proposal-comparison argument transfers the bound to an appropriately padded $O(1/d)$-accurate metric computed from high-precision Lewis weights. For spectrahedra, given $\widehat\psi\ge\psi^\star$, our implementation with the exact or a TensorSRHT-sketched log-det metric obtains the same bound with $\psi^\star$ replaced by $\widehat\psi$.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Busy Time Minimization with Preemption, Migration, and One Resource Requirement
item.description: arXiv:2609.23197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the Busy Machine Time with Preemption and Migration and One Resource Requirement problem, motivated by energy minimization in cloud data centers. Given unlimited identical-capacity machines and jobs with release times, deadlines, processing times, and resource requirements, we allow free preemption and migration at integer times and seek to minimize total machine busy time. The problem is NP-hard, and previous results consist of a 2-approximation, 2-competitive algorithm for the case of uniform heights. We obtain a 5671/2340 < 2.424-approximation algorithm and a 2.5-competitive online algorithm, both running in O(n^2 log n) time. Our methods are based on new non-asymptotic performance bounds for the First Fit Decreasing algorithm for Bin Packing, and a new generalization of Span Minimization, the Huge-Tiny Busy Time problem, for which we present an exact offline algorithm and an optimal (3/2)-competitive deterministic online algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Gruia Calinescu, Mozhengfu Liu

item.title: Parameterized Complexity of Spanner Problems with Independent Weights and Lengths
item.description: arXiv:2609.29259v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, the parameterized complexity of the multiplicative $\alpha$-spanner problem with independent weights and lengths on undirected graphs is considered for the first time. All prior FPT results (except one on DAGs) assume basic instances (i.e., with unit weights and lengths) and are parameterized in the stretch factor $\alpha$ and the (in practice typically non-constant) number of removed edges. We show that several parameterizations do not allow FPT algorithms. However, our exclusion approach generalizes an existing algorithm for basic instances to arbitrary weights and lengths. It is parameterized by the total removed weight and a new tightness parameter. The latter is more precise than $\alpha$ and allows us to also improve the best known result for basic instances. Our second algorithm, called inclusion approach, uses the natural parameterization in the spanner's total weight. We prove that this sole parameter leaves a W[2]-hard problem, but also show FPT algorithms exist when augmented with secondary parameters.
item.dc:creator: Marius B\"achler, Markus Chimani, Henning Jasper

item.title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.09392v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$ O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. A direct implementation on a deterministic Turing machine with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, \log^2 n$ steps. Thus both models have polynomial degree $94$ for three machines, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.
item.dc:creator: Klaus Jansen

item.title: The Approximation Ratio of $k$-means++ Is $2\ln k+O(1)$
item.description: arXiv:2611.14573v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given a finite set of points in Euclidean space, $k$-means clustering seeks $k$ centers that minimize the sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest center. The $k$-means++ algorithm chooses its first center uniformly at random from the data points and each subsequent center with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest center already chosen. Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove that $R_k=2\ln k+O(1)$; more precisely, $2H_{k-1}+2\le R_k\le 2H_{k-2}+5$ for $k\ge2$, where $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number, so the two bounds differ by less than $3$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$, with a unified proof of both upper bounds, and give a second family of lower bounds that exceeds $2H_{k-1}+2$ for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit. At each subsequent draw, the probability of sampling that cluster again is exactly its share of the current cost. We show that the cost reductions from these later hits suffice, in expectation, to bring the leading coefficient down to $2$.
item.dc:creator: Aravind Reddy

item.title: Generalized De Bruijn Words, Invertible Necklaces, and the Burrows-Wheeler Transform
item.description: arXiv:2502.12844v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We define generalized de Bruijn words as those words having a Burrows--Wheeler transform that is a concatenation of permutations of the alphabet. We show that generalized de Bruijn words are in one-to-one correspondence with Hamiltonian cycles in the generalized de Bruijn graphs, introduced in the early 1980s in the context of network design. We prove that generalized de Bruijn words retain the asymptotically maximal factor complexity of ordinary de Bruijn words over a fixed alphabet. We then use this class to construct an infinite binary family on which the Burrows--Wheeler transform reduces this complexity from asymptotically maximal to the constant $2$. In particular, this shows that the BWT can substantially improve dictionary compressibility. When the size of the alphabet is a prime $p$, we define invertible necklaces as those whose BWT-matrix is nonsingular. We show that invertible necklaces of length $n$ correspond to normal bases of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p^n}$, and that they form an abelian group isomorphic to the Reutenauer group $RG_p^n$. Using known results in abstract algebra, we can establish a connection between generalized de Bruijn words and invertible necklaces. In particular, we highlight a correspondence between binary de Bruijn words of order $d+1$, binary necklaces of length $2^{d}$ having an odd number of $1$'s, invertible BWT matrices of size $2^{d}\times 2^{d}$, and normal bases of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{2^{2^{d}}}$.
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Fici, Est\'eban Gabory

item.title: Rapid Mixing of Glauber Dynamics for Monotone Systems via Entropic Independence
item.description: arXiv:2507.11031v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the mixing time of Glauber dynamics on monotone systems. For monotone systems satisfying the entropic independence condition, we prove a new mixing time comparison result for Glauber dynamics. For concrete applications, we obtain mixing time bounds from specified extremal configurations: $\tilde{O}(n)$ for the random cluster model induced by the ferromagnetic Ising model with consistently biased external fields, and $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ for the bipartite hardcore model under the one-sided uniqueness condition, where $n$ is the number of variables in the corresponding models, improving the best known results in [Chen and Zhang, SODA'23] and [Chen, Liu, and Yin, FOCS'23], respectively. Our proof combines ideas from the stochastic dominance argument in the classical censoring inequality and the recently developed high-dimensional expanders. The key step in the proof is a novel comparison result between the Glauber dynamics and the field dynamics for monotone systems.
item.dc:creator: Weiming Feng, Minji Yang

item.title: Fine-Grained Hardness of Approximating Dynamic Time Warping
item.description: arXiv:2610.09233v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove conditional lower bounds for approximating dynamic time warping (DTW) over the uniform metric. Let $N,M$ be the lengths of the two strings and $n,m$ their numbers of runs. Under the Gap Block Disjointness Hypothesis, no deterministic algorithm $O(N^{\varepsilon})$-approximates DTW on two strings of length $N$ over three symbols in $\widetilde O(N^{2-\delta})$ time for any constants $\delta\in(0,1]$ and $\varepsilon\in[0,\delta/3)$. In particular, no deterministic constant-factor approximation runs in strongly subquadratic time. For run-length encoded strings with $n=m$, the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis rules out every constant-factor approximation in $\widetilde O((nm)^{1-\delta})$ time for every constant $\delta>0$. It also rules out $(N+M)^{1-\eta}$-approximation in this time for every constant $\eta\in(0,1)$. The bounds extend to every fixed metric with at least three points, including absolute distance on $\{0,1,2\}$. Both reductions use long runs to force equal-symbol matches on low-cost paths. For explicit strings, Boolean gadgets encode the source predicate. A deterministic disperser-based density amplification then yields the polynomial gap. For run-length encoded strings, we encode regular-expression membership so that the gap grows without adding runs.
item.dc:creator: Jihan Wang
